questions.stem: A regional operations manager runs a Project that turns site inspection notes into reports. The Project instructions say 'Keep every report under 250 words' and also 'Always follow the approved template'. The template, stored as a knowledge file, has seven mandatory sections. Reports now regularly drop the last two or three sections while staying under 250 words, and rewording each request has not helped. What is the MOST effective fix?

options.text: Switch to the most capable model available so it can fit all seven sections into 250 words without dropping any content.
Add 'DO NOT SKIP ANY SECTIONS' in capitals at the top of the instructions and leave the word limit unchanged.
Decide which rule wins (raise the limit or cap each section), update the instructions, then retest on past notes.
Remove the template from the knowledge files so Claude stops trying to follow two sources of guidance at once.

questions.explanation: The symptom (sections dropped, word limit respected) points to **two instructions that cannot both be met**. Seven mandatory sections may not fit in 250 words, so Claude keeps one rule and sacrifices the other. Rewording the request can't fix a conflict that lives in the Project instructions. The fix is to decide the priority at the source, for example a higher overall limit or a short length per section, then **rerun a few past inspection notes** to confirm all seven sections now appear and nothing else broke.

whyWrong.A: No model can satisfy two rules that contradict each other. A bigger model would still have to choose between the word limit and the template, so the root cause stays in place.
whyWrong.B: Shouting the rule louder doesn't remove the conflict. The word limit and the seven mandatory sections still cannot both be satisfied, so Claude must still break one of them — and now it has three emphatic instructions to juggle instead of two clear ones.
whyWrong.D: The template is the mandatory structure the business needs. Deleting it 'resolves' the conflict by abandoning the requirement instead of reconciling it.

questions.mindset: When two instructions can't both be satisfied, fix the conflict at the source rather than adding louder rules.

questions.stem: A grants officer types her request first ('Summarize only the eligibility criteria as a checklist; ignore the budget guidance') and then pastes a 60-page funding call below it in the same message. Claude replies with a general summary of the whole call, budget guidance included. She wants a more reliable result with minimal extra effort on future calls. Which TWO changes are MOST likely to help? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to end each reply by rating from 1 to 10 how closely it followed her original instructions.
Paste the full funding call first, then put her instructions and question after it at the end of the message.
Switch to a lighter, faster model, since long documents make the more capable models drift off the task.
Split the funding call into sixty separate single-page messages and request an eligibility checklist for each page.
Wrap the pasted call in clearly labeled tags, such as <funding_call>, so it sits visibly apart from her request.

questions.explanation: Her instruction was buried: a short request followed by 60 pages of text, with nothing marking where the instructions end and the material begins. Anthropic's long-context guidance recommends putting **long documents at the top and the query at the end**, and using **XML-style tags** to separate material from instructions. Both are small, reusable changes that address the cause directly, and she can apply them to every future funding call.

whyWrong.A: A self-rating is not evidence. Claude can give itself a high score on a reply that still includes the budget guidance, and the rating does nothing to fix how the prompt is laid out.
whyWrong.C: Model size isn't the cause, and the documentation gives no basis for lighter models handling buried instructions better. The prompt's structure is the problem.
whyWrong.D: Sixty messages is a big jump in effort and usage, and it breaks cross-references between pages (eligibility rules often span sections). It is an over-engineered response to a layout problem.

questions.mindset: Long material first, clear instructions last, and labels in between: structure fixes buried instructions.

questions.stem: A communications officer drafts speaking notes that a senior leader will read aloud at a staff town hall. Her prompt says 'Don't use bullet points, headings or bold text.' About half of the drafts still come back with headings and bulleted lists. Which change is MOST likely to fix this?

options.text: State the target and the reason: 'Write flowing spoken paragraphs, because the leader will read this aloud.'
Repeat the ban three times in the prompt: once at the start, once in the middle and once at the end.
Regenerate each draft until one arrives without headings, then save that version for the leader to read.
Ask Claude for a table of talking points first, then have it convert that table into prose in a second message.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's prompting guidance says to **tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do**, and to explain **why** a rule matters so Claude can generalize from it. 'Don't use bullets' names what to avoid but not what to produce. 'Flowing spoken paragraphs, because it will be read aloud' gives a clear target and a reason, and the reason also steers word choice toward something easy to say.

whyWrong.B: Repeating a negative instruction still gives no picture of the desired output. Claude knows what to avoid but not what to aim for.
whyWrong.C: Regenerating until one draft happens to come out right isn't repeatable. Next week's notes will hit the same problem.
whyWrong.D: Asking for a table first introduces exactly the kind of structure she wants to avoid and adds an extra step, while the real fix is a positive instruction with the reason.

questions.mindset: Describe the output you want and why, not just the output you don't want.

questions.stem: A retail marketing coordinator gives Claude three example social posts so that new posts match the brand voice. All three examples promote the same spring garden sale, and each ends with the same emoji and hashtag. New posts about winter coats and kitchenware now slip in gardening references and reuse that exact closing line. What is the BEST adjustment?

options.text: Remove all three examples and describe the brand voice instead with a longer paragraph of adjectives.
Add a fourth example about the same garden sale so Claude has more material to learn the voice from.
Switch to the most capable model so it can work out which parts of the examples are meant to be copied.
Use varied examples across products and closing lines, and label them as illustrations of voice only.

questions.explanation: Examples are one of the strongest ways to steer tone and structure, but Claude also picks up **patterns you didn't intend**. When every example shares the same topic and sign-off, those details look like part of the format. Anthropic's guidance says examples should be **relevant and diverse** and clearly marked as examples. Varying the products and closings shows which features are the voice (keep) and which are incidental (vary).

whyWrong.A: Dropping examples throws away the most reliable lever for voice. Adjectives like 'friendly but premium' are far vaguer than a few well-chosen examples.
whyWrong.B: Another garden-sale example makes the unwanted pattern stronger, not weaker.
whyWrong.C: The examples send a misleading signal, and a bigger model reads that same signal. The fix is better examples, not a bigger model.

questions.mindset: Claude copies what your examples have in common, so make sure only the intended features are shared.

questions.stem: A customer service team lead pastes three things into one message as unlabeled plain text: a complaint email from Customer A, an older email from Customer B for background, and the company's reply guidelines. She then writes 'Draft a reply.' Claude's draft answers Customer B's question and quotes a guideline as though the customer had written it. What should she do FIRST?

options.text: Send the identical message again, because a fresh attempt will probably pick the correct email to answer.
Label each piece (for example <complaint>, <background>, <guidelines>) and say which one to reply to.
Remove the guidelines from the message, since policy text tends to confuse Claude when drafting customer replies.
Ask Claude to explain its reasoning, then correct it across a long follow-up chat until it understands.

questions.explanation: The output mixed up **whose email is whose** and **which text is guidance**. That is the classic sign of unseparated inputs. Wrapping each kind of content in its own tag and naming the one to answer removes the ambiguity. Anthropic recommends XML-style tags exactly when a prompt mixes instructions, context and variable inputs.

whyWrong.A: The input is still ambiguous, so a retry is a coin toss and the same mix-up can happen next time.
whyWrong.C: The guidelines are needed for a compliant reply. The problem is that they weren't marked as guidelines, not that they were included.
whyWrong.D: A long corrective conversation spends time and usage and still doesn't fix the template she will reuse for the next complaint.

questions.mindset: When several inputs share one message, label them so Claude knows which is which.

questions.stem: A finance assistant uploads a 4,000-row expense spreadsheet and asks Claude for total spend by department. The written summary reads well, but two department totals don't match the figures her manager calculated. The totals will be presented at a budget review next week. Which TWO actions BEST address this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Confirm code execution and file creation are on, and ask Claude to compute totals with code and show its method.
Ask Claude to re-read the whole spreadsheet carefully and confirm that it is now fully confident the totals are right.
Copy all 4,000 rows into the chat as plain text so Claude can see every number directly in the conversation.
Before the review, spot-check the totals against a pivot table or filtered sum in the spreadsheet itself.
Switch to the largest, most capable model and request the same written summary of department totals again.

questions.explanation: Two totals out of line on a large dataset suggest the arithmetic was not done reliably. In Claude's apps, the **code execution and file creation** capability lets Claude process spreadsheet files with code, which gives exact sums and a method you can inspect. Because the figures go to a budget review, a **human check against an independent calculation** is still needed. Claude shouldn't be the only source of truth for high-stakes numbers.

whyWrong.B: Stated confidence is not verification. Claude can sound certain about a wrong total, and nothing about how the numbers are calculated has changed.
whyWrong.C: Pasting the rows as text uses much more of the conversation and still leaves the sums to be estimated in prose. It changes the format, not the method.
whyWrong.E: A larger model may still produce the totals without computing them, and nothing in this option adds a check before the review.

questions.mindset: For numbers, have them computed and then check them independently. Don't take the model's word for it.

questions.stem: A UX researcher asks Claude to pull 'the five strongest customer quotes about onboarding' from twelve interview transcripts for a leadership presentation. When she checks, two of the quotes are polished paraphrases that no participant actually said, and one is attributed to the wrong participant. Which TWO changes are MOST effective? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add 'be accurate and do not make anything up' to the prompt and keep the rest of the request the same.
Ask Claude to smooth the quotes into natural-sounding language so any paraphrasing is less noticeable to readers.
Ask for word-for-word quotes with transcript name and location, and allow 'none found' as an answer.
Ask Claude to rate each quote's accuracy from 1 to 5 and keep only the quotes that are rated 4 or higher.
Check every selected quote against its source transcript before it goes into the leadership presentation.

questions.explanation: Invented or misattributed quotes are hallucinations. Anthropic's guidance for reducing them includes asking for **direct, word-for-word quotes** tied to their source and **giving Claude permission to say it can't find something**, so it isn't pushed to fill the gap. Those techniques reduce hallucinations but don't eliminate them, so quotes headed to leadership still need a **human check against the transcripts**.

whyWrong.A: A general 'be accurate' gives Claude no new method or permission to come up short. The request still pushes for five strong quotes whether or not they exist.
whyWrong.B: This hides the problem instead of fixing it. Presenting paraphrases as customer quotes misleads leadership.
whyWrong.D: A self-assigned accuracy score is not evidence. Claude can rate a fabricated quote highly, and the score doesn't compare anything against the transcripts.

questions.mindset: Ground quotes in exact source text, allow 'not found', and verify before an audience sees them.

questions.stem: A compliance coordinator asks Claude, in a regular chat with no files attached, to summarize the reporting deadlines in an industry rule that was amended two months ago. Claude confidently describes the deadlines as they were before the amendment. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Ask Claude whether it is fully sure about the deadlines and accept the summary if it says that it is.
Switch to the most capable model, since it will have more up-to-date knowledge of the amended rule.
Give Claude the current rule text (upload it or turn on web search) and ask it to summarize only from that source.
Add 'use the latest version of the rule' to the prompt and ask for exactly the same summary once again.

questions.explanation: This is **stale knowledge**: Claude's built-in knowledge comes from its training data and can miss recent changes. The fix is to supply the current source, either by uploading the amended text or by turning on **web search**, and to ask Claude to answer only from that source. Then check the summary against the source before relying on it for compliance work.

whyWrong.A: Asking Claude if it's sure doesn't give it new information. It may simply restate the outdated deadlines with the same confidence.
whyWrong.B: Every model's knowledge comes from training data with a cutoff. A more capable model is not guaranteed to know about a recent amendment, and the safe fix is a current source either way.
whyWrong.D: Claude can't use a version it has never seen. The instruction just asks it to guess what changed.

questions.mindset: For recent or changing facts, bring the current source to Claude instead of relying on what it already knows.

questions.stem: An IT service desk lead uses a Project in which Claude tags incoming staff requests as 'urgent', 'normal' or 'low'. The instructions simply say 'Tag urgency appropriately.' Reviewing a week of output, she finds nearly identical requests, such as 'laptop won't start, client meeting in an hour', tagged urgent one day and normal the next. What is the MOST effective fix?

options.text: Define each label with clear criteria and add varied tagged examples, including borderline cases.
Ask Claude to explain its reasoning for each tag so she can see why the labels change from day to day.
Regenerate any tag that looks wrong until it matches the label she would have chosen for that request herself.
Start a fresh chat every morning so the previous day's tagging decisions cannot influence today's labels.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent answers to the same kind of input usually mean the **criteria are undefined**. 'Appropriately' leaves Claude to reinvent the standard each time. Anthropic's consistency guidance recommends specifying the expected output precisely and **constraining with examples**. Putting criteria (for example, 'urgent = blocks client-facing work within 4 hours') and a few varied examples, including edge cases, in the Project instructions makes the standard durable for every chat.

whyWrong.B: Explanations might help her see why the tags vary, but they don't change the vague standard, so the inconsistency continues.
whyWrong.C: Fixing tags by hand doesn't scale and doesn't stop the next week's inconsistency. The correction never reaches the instructions.
whyWrong.D: The variation comes from an undefined standard, not from leftover context. A fresh chat with the same vague instruction varies in the same way.

questions.mindset: Inconsistent output usually means an undefined standard, so write the criteria down and show examples.

questions.stem: An HR business partner's Project instructions include: 'CRITICAL: You MUST ALWAYS add the full employment-advice disclaimer to EVERY response.' Claude now attaches the long disclaimer even to quick tasks like rewording a meeting invite, and colleagues delete it by hand. Policy requires the disclaimer only when a reply discusses an employee's rights or entitlements. What is the BEST change?

options.text: Delete the disclaimer rule entirely and rely on colleagues to add the text themselves whenever it is needed.
Rewrite the rule calmly with its trigger and reason: add it when a reply covers rights or entitlements, as policy requires.
Keep the rule as written and add a second CRITICAL rule saying never to add the disclaimer to short replies.
Switch to a lighter model, which tends to follow instructions less strictly when the reply is a casual one.

questions.explanation: Claude is following the instruction, not failing to follow it: the rule demands the disclaimer on **every** response, and the capitals and 'MUST ALWAYS' only underline that blanket scope. Policy requires the disclaimer just for replies about rights or entitlements, so the rule is missing its real trigger. Rewriting it calmly — 'Add the full disclaimer when the reply discusses an employee's rights or entitlements, because policy requires it' — states the condition and the reason. Anthropic's guidance is to be clear and direct about exactly what you want, and to explain **why** a rule exists so Claude can apply it sensibly in cases the wording doesn't spell out.

whyWrong.A: This removes a policy-required safeguard and makes compliance depend on memory. The disclaimer is needed in some replies.
whyWrong.C: Two emphatic, overlapping rules conflict ('always' and 'never'), and a short reply about entitlements would leave Claude unsure which to follow.
whyWrong.D: Relying on a model to follow instructions less reliably is not a control. The disclaimer could then go missing exactly where policy needs it.

questions.mindset: Give a rule its real trigger and its reason in calm language; volume isn't precision.

questions.stem: A project coordinator asks Claude, in a single message, to write a complete 30-section onboarding handbook from a long set of notes. The early sections are detailed, but later ones are thin, a few are missing, and the closing checklist refers to sections that don't exist. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Send the same request again with 'make every section equally detailed' added to the end of the prompt.
Ask for a 10-section handbook instead, so the whole document fits comfortably in a single response.
Switch to Research mode so Claude can gather more background information before writing all 30 sections.
Ask for an outline first, approve it, then have Claude draft a few sections at a time against it.

questions.explanation: Thinning, missing sections and broken cross-references are signs that the **task is too big for one request**. Decomposition fixes it: an approved outline fixes the structure (so the checklist can point at real sections), and drafting a few sections at a time gives each part full attention. Anthropic's guidance recommends breaking complex tasks into smaller subtasks and chaining prompts for exactly this reason.

whyWrong.A: One extra line doesn't change the size of the job. The same single request will run into the same thinning and inconsistency.
whyWrong.B: This shrinks the requirement instead of meeting it. The team needs 30 sections, not 10.
whyWrong.C: The notes already hold the content. The failure is in producing a long deliverable in one pass, not in gathering information, and Research mode adds time and usage.

questions.mindset: When a big deliverable falls apart near the end, break it up: outline, approve, then build it piece by piece.

questions.stem: A store operations manager set up a Project with the company's returns policy as a knowledge file. When staff ask about returning opened electronics, Claude sometimes gives a typical industry answer, such as a 14-day window, that differs from the 30-day rule in the company's file. Which change is MOST likely to fix this?

options.text: Upload two extra copies of the returns policy so Claude encounters the company's own rules more often.
Tell staff to add 'please check carefully' at the end of every returns question they ask in the Project.
Have the instructions say to answer returns questions only from the policy file, cite the section, and flag gaps.
Switch the Project to the most capable model, which is better at recalling company-specific policies.

questions.explanation: Claude is filling in from **general knowledge** instead of the company source. Anthropic's hallucination guidance recommends **restricting Claude to the provided documents**, asking for a citation to the supporting text, and allowing it to say when the source doesn't cover a question. Putting this in the Project instructions makes it apply to every staff question, and the cited section lets staff check the answer quickly.

whyWrong.A: Duplicate files add clutter without telling Claude to prefer them over general knowledge. Duplicates can also cause version confusion later.
whyWrong.B: A courtesy phrase is cosmetic. It doesn't tell Claude which source to use or what to do when the file is silent.
whyWrong.D: Company-specific policy isn't something any model learned in training. The fix is grounding in the file, not a bigger model.

questions.mindset: If the answer must come from your document, say so explicitly and ask for the section it came from.

questions.stem: A marketing team's Project produced reliable weekly campaign summaries for months. Last week a colleague edited the instructions, added four knowledge files and changed the model, all at once. Summaries are now padded and leave out the conversion figures. The team still has last month's instructions and several past inputs with approved outputs. What should they do FIRST to diagnose the problem?

options.text: Restore the last known-good setup, rerun the saved inputs, then add each change back one at a time and compare outputs.
Rewrite the instructions from scratch with stronger wording about conversion figures and keep the other changes.
Ask Claude which of last week's changes caused the drop in quality, then apply the fix that it suggests.
Keep the new setup but regenerate each weekly summary several times and choose the best version each week.

questions.explanation: Three variables changed at once, so nobody knows which one caused the regression. The disciplined move is to **change one thing at a time**: confirm the old setup still produces the approved outputs on the saved inputs, then reintroduce each change and compare against the same criteria. The saved inputs and approved outputs act as a small test set, which is the lightweight version of Anthropic's advice to define success criteria and test against them.

whyWrong.B: This adds a fourth change on top of three untested ones. Even if it helps, the team won't know what broke, and the padding may persist.
whyWrong.C: Claude can offer guesses, but it has no reliable view of which configuration change caused the drop. The answer comes from controlled comparison, not self-diagnosis.
whyWrong.D: Regenerating hides the regression and costs extra effort every week, while the cause stays in the setup.

questions.mindset: When quality drops after several changes, go back to what worked and add the changes back one at a time.

questions.stem: A people-operations analyst needs a balanced briefing for leaders who are deciding whether to pilot a four-day work week. Her prompt reads: 'Explain why a four-day week would boost our productivity.' The briefing is persuasive but mentions almost no risks or counter-evidence, and a director calls it one-sided. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Keep the prompt and add a closing line asking Claude to stay neutral and objective in tone throughout.
Reframe it neutrally: ask for the strongest evidence for and against, key risks, and open questions.
Run a second prompt asking only for the downsides and send leadership the two briefings separately.
Ask Claude to cite more supporting studies so the productivity case looks better supported to directors.

questions.explanation: The bias came from the **prompt's framing**: 'explain why it would boost productivity' asks for advocacy, and Claude delivered it. A decision briefing needs both sides, so the request itself has to ask for both: evidence for and against, risks and unknowns. Being clear and direct about the actual goal (a balanced input to a decision) is the targeted fix.

whyWrong.A: A neutral tone doesn't create balance. The prompt still only asks for supporting arguments, so the content stays one-sided.
whyWrong.C: Two deliberately one-sided documents leave leaders to do the weighing themselves, and they double the work. One balanced briefing meets the need.
whyWrong.D: More supporting studies make the bias worse. The director's problem is missing counter-evidence, not weak support.

questions.mindset: A leading question gets a one-sided answer, so ask for the balance you need.

questions.stem: An office manager pastes an auto-generated meeting transcript into Claude and asks for a list of action items with owners. The transcript has timestamps but no speaker names. Several action items are assigned to the wrong people, and one owner is someone who wasn't at the meeting. Which TWO changes BEST address the root cause? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to be more careful with names and to double-check every owner before it finishes the list.
Provide a speaker-labeled transcript, or add the attendee list and clarify who said what where needed.
Switch to the most capable model so it can infer the speakers from writing style and surrounding context.
Tell Claude to mark the owner as 'Unassigned – confirm' whenever the transcript doesn't make it clear.
Ask for the action items as a table instead of a list so that any ownership errors are easier to spot.

questions.explanation: Claude can't know who said what if the input doesn't say, so it guessed, even inventing an attendee. The root cause is **missing information**. Two changes address it: **supply the missing facts** (speaker labels or an attendee list) and **give Claude permission to leave a gap** instead of guessing. Anthropic's hallucination guidance specifically recommends letting Claude admit uncertainty rather than push it to fill gaps.

whyWrong.A: Being 'careful' can't recover names that aren't in the transcript. Claude has nothing to check the owners against.
whyWrong.C: A more capable model still has to guess at speakers it can't identify, and the guesses just sound more convincing.
whyWrong.E: A table makes errors easier to scan but doesn't stop them from happening. It changes the layout, not the cause.

questions.mindset: If a fact isn't in the input, supply it or let Claude say it's unknown; never reward a guess.
